{{Short description|16-element matrix group}}
{{Dark mode invert|[[File:Pauli group-Cayley graph.svg|thumb|The [[Möbius–Kantor graph]], the [[Cayley graph]] of the Pauli group with generators {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, and {{mvar|z}}]]}}
In [[physics]], [[quantum information]] and [[group theory]], the '''Pauli group''' is a group formed by tensor products of [[Pauli matrices]], including the identity.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |first1=Artur |last1=Ekert |first2=Timothy |last2=Hosgood |first3=Alastair |last3=Kay |first4=Chiara |last4=Macchiavello |url=https://qubit.guide/7.1-pauli-groups |title=7.1 Pauli groups {{!}} Introduction to Quantum Information Science}}</ref> The single-qubit Pauli group is a 16-element [[matrix group]], consisting of the 4 Pauli matrices each with 4 possible phase factors. The {{mvar|n}}-qubit Pauli group is a <math>4^{n+1}</math>-element group consisting of tensor products of single-qubit Paulis.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bagarello |first1=Fabio |title=On the Pauli group on 2-qubits in dynamical systems with pseudofermions |date=2024 |arxiv=2308.05185 |last2=Bavuma |first2=Yanga |last3=Russo |first3=Francesco G. |journal=Forum Mathematicum |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=585–597 |doi=10.1515/forum-2022-0370 }}</ref>

In [[Quantum information science|quantum information theory]], Pauli groups are important because they are the basis for [[Stabilizer code|stabilizer formalism]], a widely-used framework for constructing and describing [[quantum error correction]] codes using sets of commuting Pauli operators. [[Stabilizer code]]s are formed from commuting subgroups of the Pauli group.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nielsen |first1=Michael A. |title=Quantum computation and quantum information |last2=Chuang |first2=Isaac L. |date=2010 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-00217-3 |edition=10th anniversary |location=Cambridge; New York}}</ref><ref>{{Cite arXiv | last1=Gottesman| first1=Daniel| title=The Heisenberg Representation of Quantum Computers| date=1998| eprint=quant-ph/9807006}}</ref>

== Single-qubit Pauli group ==
The Pauli group consists of the 2&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;2 [[identity matrix]] <math>I</math> and all of the [[Pauli matrices]]
:<math>X = \sigma_1 = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix},\quad
Y = \sigma_2 = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0&-i\\
i&0
\end{pmatrix},\quad
Z = \sigma_3 =
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&-1
\end{pmatrix}</math>,
together with the products of these matrices with the factors <math>\pm 1</math> and <math>\pm i</math>:
:<math>G \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\   \{\pm I,\pm iI,\pm X,\pm iX,\pm Y,\pm iY,\pm Z,\pm iZ\} \equiv \langle X, Y, Z \rangle</math>.
The Pauli group is [[Generating set of a group|generated]] by the Pauli matrices, and like them it is named after [[Wolfgang Pauli]].

As an abstract group, <math>G \ \cong C_4 \circ D_4</math> is the [[central product]] of a [[cyclic group]] of order 4 and the [[dihedral group]] of order 8.<ref>Pauli group on [http://groupnames.org/index.html#?Pauli GroupNames]</ref>

The Pauli group is a [[group representation|representation]] of the [[Higher-dimensional gamma matrices|gamma group]] in three-dimensional Euclidean space. It is ''not'' isomorphic to the gamma group; it is less free, in that its chiral element is <math>\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3=iI</math> whereas there is no such relationship for the gamma group.

=== Pauli algebra ===
The [[Pauli algebra]] is the [[algebra over a field|algebra]] of 2 x 2 complex matrices M(2, '''C''') with matrix addition and [[matrix multiplication]]. It has a long history beginning with the [[biquaternion]]s introduced by [[W. R. Hamilton]] in his ''Lectures on Quaternions'' (1853). The representation with matrices was noted by [[L. E. Dickson]] in 1914.<ref>[[L. E. Dickson]] (1914) ''Linear Algebras'', pages 13,4</ref> Publications by Pauli eventually led to the [[eponym]] now in use. [[Basis (linear algebra)|Basis]] elements of the algebra generate the Pauli group.

== Multi-qubit Pauli group ==
The Pauli group on <math>n</math> [[qubit]]s, <math>G_n</math>, is the group generated by the operators described above applied to each of <math>n</math> qubits in the [[tensor product]] [[Hilbert space]] <math>(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}</math>. That is,

<math display="block">
G_n = \langle P_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes P_n : P_i \in \{I, X, Y, Z \} \rangle = \{ c \cdot P_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes P_n : c \in \{\pm 1, \pm i\}, P_i \in \{I, X, Y, Z \} \}.
</math>

The [[Order (group theory)|order]] of <math>G_n</math> is <math>4 \cdot 4^n</math> since a scalar <math>\pm 1</math> or <math>\pm i</math> factor in any tensor position can be moved to any other position.

=== Notations ===
An <math>n</math>-qubit Pauli operator that only acts on a single qubit is often denoted as a single Pauli letter with an integer subscript. For example, in a system with 3 qubits,
:<math>X_1 \equiv X \otimes I \otimes I, \qquad Z_2 \equiv I \otimes Z \otimes I.</math>
Multi-qubit Pauli operators can be written as products of single-qubit Paulis on disjoint qubits. Alternatively, when it is clear from context, the tensor product symbol <math>\otimes</math> can be omitted, i.e. unsubscripted Pauli matrices written consecutively represents tensor product rather than matrix product. For example:
:<math>XZI \equiv X_1Z_2 = X \otimes Z \otimes I.</math>

=== Properties ===
Operators in <math>G_n</math> can also be represented as <math>2^n \times 2^n</math> matrices. An operator <math>P = c \cdot P_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes P_n</math> always has two distinct [[eigenvalue]]s, either <math>\pm 1</math> or <math>\pm i</math> depending on whether the scalar factor <math>c</math> is <math>\pm 1</math> or <math>\pm i</math>. An operator with eigenvalues <math>\pm 1</math> is [[Self-adjoint operator|Hermitian]], and one with eigenvalues <math>\pm i</math> is anti-Hermitian. In either case, a set of <math>2^n</math> eigenvectors of <math>P</math> can be constructed by taking tensor products of eigenvectors of each <math>P_i</math>, with the eigenvalue being <math>c</math> times the product of the eigenvalues of each factor.

Two operators in <math>G_n</math> either [[Commutative property|commute]] or [[anti-commute]], depending on whether the number of anti-commuting pairs of single-qubit Pauli operators at the same location is even or odd. For example, <math>XXX</math> and <math>ZZX</math> commute with each other since there are exactly two anti-commuting pairs (on qubits 1 and 2), but <math>XXX</math> and <math>ZZZ</math> anti-commute since there are three such pairs.

=== Binary vector representation ===

A simple but useful mapping <math>N</math> exists between the binary [[vector space]] {{tmath|(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2} }} and the set of Pauli matrices {{tmath|\{I, X, Y, Z\} }}:

:{{tmath|00 \to I, \; 01 \to X, \; 11 \to Y, \; 10 \to Z.}}

This mapping allows a multi-qubit Pauli operator to be represented as a [[bit vector|binary vector]]s with a phase factor, and operations on these operators to be defined as [[binary operation]]s rather than [[matrix operation]]s.

Some useful properties of this mapping becomes evident when the phaseless Pauli operators {{tmath|I, X, Y, Z}} are regarded as representatives of [[equivalence class]]es in the [[quotient group]] {{tmath|1=[G] = G / \{\pm 1, \pm i\} }} (where {{tmath|G}} is the single-qubit Pauli group). For {{tmath|P \in G}}, denote the equivalence class represented by {{tmath|P}} as
:{{tmath|1=
[P] = \{\beta P \mid \beta \in \{\pm 1, \pm i\}\}. 
}}
Note that {{tmath|[G]}} is a [[commutative group]] since two Pauli operators either commute or anti-commute, but {{tmath|1=[-P] = [P]}}.

The map {{tmath|N}} now induces an [[isomorphism]] {{tmath|[N] : (\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2} \mapsto [G]}}, i.e., addition of vectors in {{tmath|(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2} }} is equivalent to multiplication of Pauli operators up to a global phase:
:{{tmath|1=
[N(u + v)] = [N(u)][N(v)].
}}

Furthermore, let {{tmath|\odot}} denote the [[symplectic product]] between two elements {{tmath|u, v \in (\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2} }}, where {{tmath|1=u = z \vert x}} and {{tmath|1=v = z' \vert x'}} (this notation represents binary string concatenation, e.g., {{tmath|01 \equiv 0 \vert 1}}), {{tmath|z, x, z', x' \in \mathbb{Z}_{2} }}:
:{{tmath|
u \odot v \equiv zx' - xz'.
}}

Then the symplectic product {{tmath|\odot}} gives the [[Commutative property|commutation]] relations of elements of {{tmath|G}}:
:{{tmath|1=
N(u)N(v) = (-1)^{(u \odot v)}N(v)N(u).
}}

The symplectic product and the mapping {{tmath|N}} thus give a useful way to phrase Pauli relations in terms of [[Boolean algebra (logic)|binary algebra]].

The above definitions can be straightforwardly extended to multiple qubits, defining a mapping {{tmath|\mathbf{N} : (\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2n} \mapsto G_n}} such that
:{{tmath|1=
\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{z} \vert \mathbf{x}) = N(z_1 \vert x_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes N(z_n \vert x_n).
}}

Similar to the single-qubit case, denoting the quotient group {{tmath|G_n / \{\pm 1, \pm i\} }} as {{tmath|[G_n]}}, the map {{tmath|[\mathbf{N}] : (\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2n} \mapsto [G_n]}} is an isomorphism:
:{{tmath|1=
[\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})] = [\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{u})][\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{v})].
}}

Furthermore, for {{tmath|1=\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{z} \vert \mathbf{x} }} and {{tmath|1=\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{z}' \vert \mathbf{x}'}}, where {{tmath|\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}', \mathbf{x}' \in (\mathbb{Z}_{2})^n}}, define the symplectic product {{tmath|\odot}} as 
:{{tmath|1=
\mathbf{u}\odot\mathbf{v} \equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}'-x_{i}
z_{i}' = \sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}\odot v_{i},
}}
where {{tmath|1=u_{i} = z_{i} \vert x_{i} }} and {{tmath|1=v_{i} = z_{i}' \vert x_{i}'}}. Then the symplectic product captures the commutation relations of any operators {{tmath|\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{u})}} and {{tmath|\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{v})}}:
:{{tmath|1=
\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{v}) = (-1)^{(\mathbf{u}\odot\mathbf{v})  }\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{v})\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{u}).
}}

The above binary representation and [[symplectic algebra]] are especially useful in making the relation between classical linear [[error correction]] and quantum [[stabilizer code]]s more explicit. In the language of [[symplectic vector space]]s, a [[Symplectic vector space#Subspaces|symplectic]] subspace corresponds to a [[direct sum]] of Pauli algebras (i.e., encoded qubits), while an [[Symplectic vector space#Subspaces|isotropic]] subspace corresponds to a set of stabilizers.
